content:
# XAMPP Error: www.example.com:443:0 server certificate does NOT include an ID which matches the server name

This Apache error message is a classic symptom of a mismatch between your SSL configuration and the actual certificate you are serving. When Apache starts up, it validates that the Common Name (CN) or Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in your SSL certificate file matches the hostname you defined in your virtual host configuration. If they don't align, Apache logs a warning like `AH01909: www.example.com:443:0 server certificate does NOT include an ID which matches the server name`.

While this often manifests as a generic "certificate mismatch" in browser consoles, it can also cause strict HTTP clientsâlike Android's Volley libraryâto fail requests entirely, returning a status code of `0` or throwing handshake exceptions. This happens because modern TLS implementations are increasingly strict about hostname verification to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. Even if Postman works, which it often does by relaxing certificate validation rules or ignoring the specific hostname check, your production client will not be as forgiving.

The root cause is almost certainly that you are using a self-signed certificate generated with a placeholder name (like `localhost` or `test.local`) while trying to serve traffic on a custom domain like `www.example.com`. In XAMPP, this usually stems from the default SSL configuration files located in `C:\xampp\apache\conf\extra\ssl.conf` or within your specific virtual host definition in `httpd-vhosts.conf`.

To resolve this, you must ensure the certificate identity matches your intended domain. If you are testing locally and cannot obtain a commercial SSL certificate for `www.example.com`, you have two primary paths: generate a self-signed certificate with the correct Common Name, or configure Apache to use `localhost` as the server name while accessing the site via IP address or `localhost`.

### Generating a Certificate with the Correct Identity

The most robust fix is to regenerate your SSL certificate ensuring the metadata matches your target domain. You can do this using OpenSSL directly on Windows. Navigate to your XAMPP installation directory and open a Command Prompt there. Run the following command to create a new certificate key pair:

```bash
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout server.key -out server.crt
```

When prompted for the `Common Name (FQDN)`, you must type exactly `www.example.com`. If you type `localhost` here, Apache will continue to complain when you try to access `www.example.com`. You also need to fill in other details like organization or country; these are metadata and less critical for a local development environment.

Once the generation completes, locate the new files (`server.key` and `server.crt`) in your XAMPP directory (typically `C:\xampp\apache\conf\extra`). Replace the existing certificate files with these new ones. Restart the Apache service via the XAMPP Control Panel to apply the changes.

### Configuring the Virtual Host

If you are using named virtual hosts, ensure that the `SSLCertificateFile` and `SSLCertificateKeyFile` directives in your `.conf` file point to the files you just generated. Your configuration block should look similar to this:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:443>
    DocumentRoot "C:/xampp/htdocs/www.example.com"
    ServerName www.example.com
    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile "C:/xampp/apache/conf/extra/server.crt"
    SSLCertificateKeyFile "C:/xampp/apache/conf/extra/server.key"
</VirtualHost>
```

Notice the `ServerName` directive. This must match the Common Name in your certificate exactly. If your certificate is for `www.example.com`, but your `ServerName` is set to `localhost`, Apache will log the mismatch error you are seeing.

### Trade-offs and Limitations

If your goal is purely local development without needing a specific domain name, you can simplify the setup by changing your virtual host's `ServerName` to `localhost` and generating a certificate with `CN=localhost`. In this scenario, your Android app or any client must connect to `http://localhost:443`. This eliminates the mismatch error but requires updating your application's configuration to stop using the external domain name.

It is important to note that XAMPP's default SSL setup often relies on pre-generated certificates that are not suitable for custom domains. Unlike production-grade setups where you might use Let's Encrypt or a corporate CA, XAMPP defaults can be inflexible regarding certificate identities unless manually overridden. Always verify the contents of your certificate using `openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject` to confirm the Common Name before restarting Apache.

By aligning the certificate identity with your server configuration, you restore strict hostname verification, allowing clients like Volley to complete the TLS handshake successfully and receive the expected JSON responses instead of failing silently.
